raw_response:
Well, another October is here. I've been farming these 6 mu for 30 years now — since I was 30 — and I know every corner of this plot. My wife and I still do most of the work ourselves. Our son works in Shijiazhuang at a factory, sends a bit back now and then, but I don't count on it for buying inputs. The land is all we've got.

This year I'm sticking with wheat and maize on all 6 mu, same as always. Wheat-maize rotation is the only thing that makes sense here. I thought about cotton once, but with only 6 mu, if the cotton price drops, we're in trouble. At least with wheat and maize, even if one is a bit off, the other usually carries us through. Plus we need the wheat straw for the animals.

For the **winter wheat**, I'll plant around October 12th if the weather holds. I usually aim for the week after National Day. Last year I planted a bit late because of rain, and the seedlings were a bit thin. This year I'll try to get it in on time. I'm using the seed I saved from last year — Jinmai 47, an improved variety. It's reliable. Buying new seed every year is too expensive for 6 mu. I'll need about 15 jin of seed per mu, so 90 jin total. That costs me basically nothing since I saved it, just the storage.

For fertilizer, the extension guy last spring said I should do soil testing, but that costs money and I've never done it. I know my land. It's decent soil, not the best in the village. I usually put down about 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base fertilizer before planting — that's the NPK bagged stuff, about 15-15-15. Then in the spring, around Qingming or a bit after, I topdress with urea. Last year I did 10 kg of urea per mu at jointing and the wheat looked good. This year I'll probably do the same: 40 kg compound fertilizer base, then 10-12 kg urea topdress if the wheat looks yellow. I might push it to 12 kg if the early spring is dry and the wheat seems stressed. Nitrogen all together is probably around 18-20 kg per mu, phosphorus and potassium from the compound fertilizer, maybe 6 kg each. I know some guys in the village put more, but fertilizer prices went up again and I need to keep some cash for the maize season.

I'll irrigate the wheat three times if I can afford the electricity: once right after planting if it's dry, once at green-up in March, and once at jointing or grain-filling depending on rain. The well water is there, but the pump electricity isn't cheap. Last year I only did two times because the bill was getting high, and the yield was still acceptable — around 400 jin per mu. I'll aim for 450 jin per mu this year if the spring rain is decent.

Now for the **summer maize** — this is the tricky part. After I harvest the wheat in early June, I've got maybe five or six days to get the maize in the ground. I don't have my own planter, so I hire Old Wang from the next village. He charges 30 yuan per mu for planting with his machine, but it's worth it because hand-planting 6 mu in that heat would kill us. I always buy hybrid maize seed — you can't save maize seed, everyone knows that. Zhengdan 958 or something similar, whatever the seed shop has in stock. Usually about 3-4 jin per mu, costing around 40-50 yuan per mu.

For maize fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer at planting — about 35-40 kg per mu — and then topdress with urea at the big flare stage, maybe 15 kg per mu. That's less than some of the bigger farms around here, but I've found that with maize, timing matters more than amount. If I get the topdress on right when the leaves are growing fast, it does fine. Total nitrogen is probably around 16 kg per mu. Phosphorus and potassium, maybe 5 kg each from the compound fertilizer. I don't usually bother with potassium beyond what's in the compound bag.

Irrigation for maize depends on the summer rains. If July and August are normal, I might only irrigate once at the flare stage or not at all. But last July was dry, so I had to pump twice. I'll budget for one irrigation, and if it's a drought year, I'll find the money for a second. Better to irrigate than lose the whole crop.

For pesticides, I usually spray herbicide on both crops — once for wheat in the spring if the weeds are bad, and definitely on the maize because the summer weeds grow like crazy. I don't use much insecticide unless I see armyworms or something. Last year I didn't spray any insecticide and it was fine. I'll keep some on hand just in case.

Tillage is simple — after wheat harvest, I usually get Old Wang to do a quick rotavator pass before planting the maize. For wheat, I plow in the fall with my small walking tractor. I've had that thing for 15 years. It's old but it works.

Labor: my wife and I do most of it. For wheat planting and harvest, we might need 2-3 days of hired help for harvest if the weather window is tight — usually hiring local women at 120 yuan per day. For maize planting, the machine does it. Maize harvest in late September, I usually hire a combine, about 60 yuan per mu. Total family labor is probably 20 days across the whole year for these 6 mu, and hired labor maybe 4-5 days plus the machine work.

Cash is tight. Total input costs I'm looking at: wheat seed (saved, basically free), maize seed (~250 yuan), fertilizers (~800 yuan for both crops), herbicide (~150 yuan), irrigation electricity (~300 yuan), machine planting and harvest (~600 yuan). That's about 2,100 yuan. I need to make sure I have that in hand. If fertilizer prices go up more in spring, I might cut the topdress rate a bit. I'd rather under-fertilize slightly than go into debt at my age.

I expect about 450 kg per mu for wheat and 500 kg per mu for maize if the weather cooperates. That's 2,700 kg wheat and 3,000 kg maize. Last year I got a bit less because of the dry July. I'm hoping this year is kinder.
